title: Components of blood
definition: Blood is the fluid connective tissue that circulates through the heart, arteries, veins, and capillaries of the human body. It is not a simple red liquid but a complex mixture made up of two main parts: a pale, straw-coloured liquid called plasma and several types of blood cells that are suspended in it. Plasma makes up about 55 percent of the total blood volume. It is mostly water, but it also contains dissolved proteins such as albumin and fibrinogen, salts, hormones, nutrients like glucose and amino acids, and waste substances such as urea and carbon dioxide. Because it is the fluid part, plasma has the important job of transporting these materials from one part of the body to another. The blood cells that float in the plasma are of three main kinds: red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Red blood cells, also called erythrocytes or RBC, are tiny, disc-shaped cells that contain a red-coloured protein called hemoglobin. Hemoglobin picks up oxygen from the air sacs of the lungs and carries it to every living cell in the body, making red blood cells the main agents of oxygen transport. White blood cells, or WBC, are larger, fewer in number, and are the soldiers of the immune system. They protect the body from germs and foreign particles by destroying them and building immunity. Platelets, also known as thrombocytes, are not complete cells but small, irregular cell fragments. Whenever a blood vessel is cut, platelets rush to the spot and stick together to form a plug, beginning the process of clotting that prevents too much blood loss. Blood is also classified into four blood groups or blood types: A, B, AB, and O. These are determined by substances called antigens present on the surface of red blood cells. A person's blood group must be matched before a transfusion to avoid dangerous clumping. When a doctor measures blood pressure, two readings are recorded: the higher one is systolic pressure, produced when the heart contracts and pushes blood into the arteries, and the lower one is diastolic pressure, when the heart relaxes between beats. A heartbeat is the rhythmic contraction and relaxation of the heart, and the pulse is the same beat felt as a throbbing in the arteries. The pulse can easily be felt at the wrist and at the side of the neck, and its rate normally matches the heartbeat.
textWalkthrough:
In the earlier node c5_bio_002, you learned that blood is a wonderful worker inside your body. You discovered that it transports food, oxygen, and hormones, protects you from germs, and stops bleeding when you are hurt. You have already used the idea that blood does jobs. Now, in c6_bio_018, we are going one step deeper. We are asking: what is blood made of, and which part does which job? This is just like opening a delivery truck and finding the driver, the packages, and the first-aid kit.

Then, in c6_bio_017, you saw the circulatory system: the heart, the arteries, the veins, and the capillaries. Blood is the substance that moves through this road network. If the roads are the blood vessels, the trucks travelling on them are the blood. Before we study traffic signals and speed limits, we must know what those trucks are carrying and how they are built. So let us look inside the blood carefully.

First, imagine blood that has been left to settle in a tall glass tube in a hospital laboratory. The top half looks almost like pale yellow water. That is plasma. Many students think plasma is just water, but a good answer says it is the fluid part containing water, proteins, salts, digested food, hormones, and waste. A weak answer says, "Plasma is water in blood." A strong answer says, "Plasma is the liquid part of blood that transports nutrients, hormones, and waste materials." Which one would an examiner prefer?

Now, why does blood look red? Is every blood cell red? Here we meet the red blood cells, the RBC. Think of them as tiny red delivery vans. They are packed with hemoglobin, which loves oxygen. When blood passes through the lungs, hemoglobin picks up oxygen and carries it to body cells. A common mistake is to say that RBC carry food. Remember, food dissolved in plasma is carried by the liquid, while oxygen is carried by red blood cells. So, plasma is the river, and RBC are the boats loaded with oxygen.

What happens when germs enter your body? Your white blood cells, the WBC, are the police force. They are larger than RBC and can squeeze out of capillary walls to reach the place of infection. When you have a cut and it becomes swollen, you may notice that area turning red. That is partly because many WBC have rushed there to fight germs. They give you immunity, which means the power to resist disease. A good student does not write, "WBC help blood." Instead, the student writes, "WBC protect the body from infections by destroying germs and producing immunity."

Next comes the part that saves you from bleeding to death after a fall. Platelets are tiny cell fragments, not complete cells. If you cut a blood vessel, the platelets stick to the broken edges and to each other, forming a soft plug. Later, a thread-like protein called fibrin makes a net around the plug to form a solid clot. So platelets are like repair patches over a leaking pipe. A weak answer says, "Platelets stop bleeding," which is true but too short. A strong answer says, "Platelets are small cell fragments that help in clotting of blood by forming a plug at the site of injury."

Now, have you heard your elders or a doctor say someone has blood group B positive? The ABO blood groups A, B, AB, and O depend on the type of antigens on the surface of red blood cells. This matters when a patient receives blood in an Indian hospital or a blood donation camp. If the wrong blood group is given, the red blood cells may clump together and block blood vessels, which is very dangerous. The examiner only wants you to name the four groups and know that matching is important; the detailed inheritance comes later in higher classes.

Finally, let us feel the heartbeat and pulse. Place two fingers gently on the inner side of your wrist, below the thumb. Do you feel a steady throb? That is your pulse at the radial artery. You can also feel it on the side of your neck, at the carotid artery. Each throb is the result of one heartbeat pushing blood into the arteries. The pulse rate is usually the same as the heart rate. If the heart beats 70 times in one minute, the pulse will also be about 70 beats per minute. Blood pressure is measured as two numbers, like 120 over 80. The higher number is systolic pressure, when the heart contracts; the lower is diastolic pressure, when the heart relaxes. These are only concepts at this stage, so do not worry about exact calculations.

What should you remember for the board exam? The examiner will expect you to list plasma, RBC, WBC, and platelets and to give one clear function of each. They may ask you to name the four blood groups. They may also ask where the pulse can be felt and what the difference is between systolic and diastolic pressure. Avoid vague words like "blood helps the body" or "cells do work." Use the exact terms: plasma, hemoglobin, oxygen transport, immunity, clotting, heartbeat, and pulse. A good answer is always specific.
eli5: Blood is like a busy river inside you. The watery part, plasma, carries food, hormones, and waste. Floating in it are tiny red trucks called RBC that carry oxygen, white police cells called WBC that catch germs, and sticky little platelets that patch cuts. Blood comes in four groups: A, B, AB, and O. Your heart beats, and you can feel the same beat as a pulse at your wrist or neck.
misconceptionText:
Misconception 1: "Plasma is just water, and blood cells do not need it." The board examiner observations from the 2024 board exam analysis repeatedly point out that candidates give vague or partially correct answers when they fail to distinguish between a structure and its contents. Just as some students wrote "blood vessels" instead of the specific "capillaries," many students at this stage say "plasma is water in blood." The correction is that plasma is the fluid part of blood containing water, dissolved proteins, salts, nutrients, hormones, and waste products. Without this liquid transport medium, the blood cells could not move materials around the body.

Misconception 2: "RBC carry both oxygen and food, and WBC are just more red blood cells." The exam guidance also notes that candidates often write broad, vague statements such as "chemicals" instead of "enzymes," or give ambiguous answers because they have not studied the distinct roles of similar-sounding parts. In blood, students mix up the roles of RBC and WBC. The correction is that RBC contain hemoglobin and are responsible for oxygen transport, while WBC are the white blood cells that protect the body from infection and help build immunity. Food is mainly carried dissolved in the plasma, not in RBC.

Misconception 3: "A high blood pressure number means diastolic pressure, and a low number means systolic pressure." Examiner remarks for 2024 show that candidates frequently confuse closely related terms and even reverse the meanings of related concepts. The correction is that blood pressure has two readings. The higher number is the systolic pressure, which occurs when the heart contracts and pushes blood into the arteries. The lower number is the diastolic pressure, which occurs when the heart relaxes between beats.
diagnosticText:
Q1 (recall): List the four main components of blood and explain one function of each.
Answer: Blood has four main components. The first is plasma, the pale, straw-coloured fluid part of blood that makes up more than half of the total blood volume. Plasma transports dissolved nutrients such as glucose and amino acids, hormones, and waste products like urea and carbon dioxide from one part of the body to another. The second component is the red blood cell, or RBC, which contains a red pigment called hemoglobin. Hemoglobin combines with oxygen in the lungs and carries it to all the cells of the body, so RBC are responsible for oxygen transport. The third component is the white blood cell, or WBC. These cells protect the body from disease-causing germs and foreign particles by destroying them, and they help the body develop immunity. The fourth component is the platelet, a tiny, irregular cell fragment that helps in blood clotting. When a blood vessel is cut, platelets collect at the injured area and form a plug, preventing excess blood loss. Each of these parts has a special role in keeping the body healthy.

Q2 (reasoning): A child falls while playing and gets a deep cut on the knee. At first the cut bleeds a lot, but after some time the bleeding stops and a dark, hard scab forms. Which component of blood is mainly responsible for stopping the bleeding, and what is the process involved? Explain your answer step by step.
Answer: The component of blood mainly responsible for stopping the bleeding is the platelets. Platelets are not complete cells but small, irregular cell fragments present in blood. When the blood vessel in the child's knee is cut, the platelets immediately travel to the site of injury. They stick to the broken edges of the blood vessel and to one another, forming a soft, temporary plug. At the same time, plasma contains proteins such as fibrinogen, which is converted into fibrin. The fibrin forms a fine net over the plug, trapping blood cells and making the clot strong and hard. This whole process is called blood clotting. As the clot dries and hardens, it forms a scab that protects the wound while the skin heals underneath. Therefore, platelets are the main blood component that starts clotting and prevents too much blood loss. This is why even a deep cut eventually stops bleeding on its own.

Q3 (evaluate): A student says, "A person with blood group AB can donate blood to anyone because AB is the universal donor group." Evaluate this statement, giving balanced reasons for whether you agree or disagree.
Answer: This statement is not correct. A person with blood group AB is not the universal donor; instead, a person with blood group O is usually called the universal donor, while a person with blood group AB is called the universal recipient. To understand why, we must look at the antigens on red blood cells and the antibodies in plasma. A person with blood group AB has both A and B antigens on the surface of their red blood cells. If this person donates blood to someone with blood group A, the recipient's plasma already has antibodies against the B antigen. These antibodies will attack the B antigen on the donated AB red blood cells and cause them to clump together. This clumping, called agglutination, can block blood vessels and be very dangerous. On the other hand, a person with blood group O has no A or B antigens on their red blood cells, so their blood is less likely to be rejected by the recipient's immune system in emergency situations. That is why group O is often called the universal donor. Therefore, the student has confused the universal donor with the universal recipient. The statement is wrong because it ignores the antigens on the donor's red blood cells and the antibodies in the recipient's blood. Blood transfusion must always be done after proper matching, and no single group can be safely given to everyone without testing.

Q4 (apply): Your teacher asks you to count your own pulse at the wrist. Describe how you would do this correctly, and if you count 18 beats in 15 seconds, what would your pulse rate be in one minute? Explain why your pulse and heartbeat are related.
Answer: To count the pulse at the wrist, I would place the tips of two fingers, not the thumb, gently on the inner side of the wrist just below the base of the thumb. The thumb has its own strong pulse, so using the thumb might give a wrong reading. The fingers should be pressed lightly until a regular throb can be felt. I would count the number of throbs for 15 seconds and then multiply that number by 4 to get the number of beats in one minute. If I count 18 beats in 15 seconds, my pulse rate would be 18 multiplied by 4, which equals 72 beats per minute. The pulse and heartbeat are related because each heartbeat pushes a wave of blood into the arteries. This wave causes the artery wall to expand and recoil, and this is felt as the pulse. In a healthy person, the pulse rate is usually the same as the heart rate. Therefore, counting the pulse is a simple way of estimating how fast the heart is beating.

Q5 (create): Imagine that the human body is a large city and blood is the delivery and security service. Design a labelled poster showing the four components of blood as vehicles or workers in this city, and explain what each one does.
Answer: The poster would show the human body as a city with roads, homes, factories, and a police station. At the top would flow a wide, pale yellow river labelled "Plasma." The river carries food packets from the digestive factories, message slips from the hormone office, and waste bins heading to the kidneys for disposal. Floating on the river would be small red delivery vans labelled "RBC," packed with red hemoglobin oxygen tanks. They leave the lung station, travel along the roads, and deliver oxygen to every home and factory in the city. Next, white police cars labelled "WBC" would patrol the streets. When a germ or thief enters the city, the police cars rush to the spot, catch the intruder, and keep the city safe, giving the city immunity. Finally, tiny, sticky repair patches labelled "Platelets" would appear whenever a pipe along the river breaks. They would seal the crack quickly so the river does not flood the surrounding area, showing clotting. The poster would also have a small notice board showing the four blood groups A, B, AB, and O, reminding everyone that deliveries must match the right type. This creative design makes it easy to remember that each component of blood has a different and important job in the city of the body.
masteryCriteria: Can name the four components of blood (red blood cells, white blood cells, platelets, plasma) and state one function of each (RBC: carry oxygen, WBC: fight disease, platelets: clotting, plasma: transport); can explain why blood clots are important.

title: Keeping the heart healthy
definition:
Keeping the heart healthy means caring for the muscular organ that pumps blood throughout the body so that it can continue to work efficiently throughout life. The heart is a strong, hollow muscle made of cardiac muscle tissue. It beats about seventy to eighty times every minute, sending oxygen-rich blood to every cell and carrying carbon-dioxide-rich blood back to the lungs. Because the heart works without rest, it must be protected through sensible lifestyle choices. The first and most important protective habit is regular physical activity or exercise. When a child runs, cycles, swims, dances, or plays a game such as kho-kho or football, the heart muscle is exercised just like an arm or a leg muscle. With repeated activity the heart grows stronger and pumps a larger volume of blood with each beat, so it does not have to beat as fast during ordinary tasks. This improved efficiency is called cardiovascular fitness.

Good food habits also protect the heart. The body needs a balanced diet that includes fresh fruits and vegetables for vitamins, minerals, and fibre; whole grains such as chapati, brown rice, oats, ragi, and millet for energy; pulses such as moong, masoor, Bengal gram, and rajma for proteins; and a small amount of healthy fats from nuts, seeds, and oils such as mustard or groundnut oil. Water is equally important because it helps the blood flow smoothly and supports all body processes. On the other hand, too much salt can raise blood pressure, too much sugar can lead to weight gain and weakness of the heart muscle, and too much fried or junk food can increase fat and cholesterol in the blood. Cholesterol is a waxy substance that can stick to the inner walls of a blood vessel and make it narrower. When this happens, the heart has to work harder to push blood through the narrowed blood vessel.

Harmful habits that damage the heart include smoking, chewing tobacco, eating large quantities of processed or packaged foods, drinking too many sugary drinks, and sitting for long hours without movement, which is called a sedentary lifestyle. A child who watches television or plays on a mobile phone for many hours and does not play outside is not giving the heart the exercise it needs. Finally, simple everyday practices such as sleeping eight to ten hours, managing stress through hobbies and talking to family, and staying active by walking or helping with household chores keep the heart, the blood vessels, and the whole body in good condition. A healthy heart means a healthy, energetic life.
textWalkthrough:
Let us begin by remembering what you already studied in your earlier lessons. In the Class 5 chapter on the human body, c5_bio_001, you met the circulatory system. You learned that the heart is a muscular organ about the size of your fist, that it sits inside the chest, and that it has arteries and veins leading to and from it. You discovered that arteries carry blood away from the heart while veins carry blood back to it. That earlier knowledge is your foundation, because in this node, c6_bio_019, we are taking the next step: not just naming the heart, but learning how to keep it strong and efficient.

In c6_bio_017, you studied how the circulatory system works. You saw that the heart pumps blood continuously, day and night, without stopping. Blood carries oxygen and nutrients to every part of the body and collects waste such as carbon dioxide. Now think for a moment: if the heart has to beat about one hundred thousand times every day, it is like a small pump working twenty-four hours. What would happen if we made that pump work harder by blocking its pipes or by never helping the muscle grow stronger? That is the whole point of this lesson. We want to keep the pump and its pipes clean, strong, and well supplied.

Consider exercise first. Imagine two friends, Riya and Priya, who live in the same colony in Bengaluru. Riya walks to school, plays badminton in the park every evening, and helps her mother carry grocery bags. Priya mostly takes the school bus, watches cartoons, and rarely plays outside. Whose heart do you think is stronger? Riya's heart has been trained by physical activity. With each beat it can push more blood, so during normal work it beats more slowly and steadily. Priya's heart has not been trained, so even a small effort like climbing stairs makes it beat very fast. This difference is called fitness or cardiovascular fitness. A good answer in an exam might say: "Regular exercise makes the heart muscle stronger so it pumps blood more efficiently and needs fewer beats to send the same amount of blood around the body." A weak answer might merely say: "Exercise is good for the heart." The first answer explains the "how" using the words muscle, pump, and efficiently; the second does not.

Now let us think about food. Your body uses food as fuel and as building material. The heart needs the right fuel to keep its own walls and blood vessels healthy. Imagine your body as a car. If you put clean petrol in it, the engine runs smoothly. If you put dirty or thick oil in it, the pipes choke and the engine struggles. Fruits such as guava, papaya, mango, and banana, vegetables such as spinach, carrots, beetroot, and beans, and whole grains such as jowar, bajra, and ragi are like clean fuel. Fried samosas, packaged chips, sugary cola drinks, and reheated roadside pakoras are like thick, sticky oil that can leave fat inside blood vessels. A correct exam answer would be: "A balanced diet with fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and pulses gives the heart the right nutrition and keeps blood vessels free from cholesterol and fat." A weak answer would simply list "eat healthy food" without naming any items or explaining why.

Let us also look at habits that hurt the heart. Smoking is one of the most damaging. When a person smokes, the lungs cannot take in enough pure oxygen, so the blood carries less oxygen to the heart and the whole body. Smoke also damages the inner lining of blood vessels and makes cholesterol stick more easily. Chewing tobacco harms in similar ways. Then there is the sedentary lifestyle: long hours of sitting, watching screens, or sleeping too much. A sedentary lifestyle leads to weight gain and weak muscles, including the heart muscle. A good answer adds a reason: "A sedentary lifestyle makes the heart weak and can lead to obesity and high blood pressure because the body is not burning energy." A weak answer just says: "Sitting is bad." Notice the difference.

Finally, there are small daily practices that many students forget to mention. Adequate sleep lets the heart rest and the body repair itself. Managing stress through drawing, music, talking to friends, or helping at home keeps blood pressure from rising. Staying active does not always mean a sport; even sweeping the courtyard, washing your bicycle, or climbing stairs instead of the lift helps. If an exam question asks, "How will you keep your heart healthy?" a strong answer will include exercise, balanced diet, water, sleep, avoiding smoking and junk food, and staying active. A weaker answer might only write "exercise and good food." The first answer shows that the student understands the topic completely.

What can you expect in the ICSE board exam? Examiners usually ask short-answer or list-type questions on this topic: "List four habits that keep the heart healthy," or "Explain how exercise helps the heart." They expect specific, well-separated points, not the same idea repeated in different words. From board exam analysis we know that students sometimes lose marks by repeating the same point or by mixing up reasons and effects. For example, writing "exercise is good" and then writing "we should exercise" does not count as two different points. Examiners also want clean, healthy examples and simple explanations, not long, vague lists. So write each habit as a separate, complete sentence and, where you can, add the reason why it helps.
eli5: Your heart is a strong muscle that pumps blood all day. To keep it happy, play games, eat fruits and vegetables, drink water, sleep well, and do not eat too much fried food or sit for too long. When you run and play, your heart gets stronger and can pump blood more easily, just like your legs get stronger when you cycle.
misconceptionText:
Misconception 1: "If I am young, I do not need to think about heart health." Many students believe that heart problems only happen to older people. This is wrong because the heart muscle and blood vessels are affected by daily habits from childhood. If a child eats too much junk food, sits for many hours, and sleeps poorly, the heart is already being harmed. The correction is to understand that healthy habits formed in childhood protect the heart for life.

Misconception 2: "Exercise makes the heart pump faster all the time, so it is bad." Some students think that because the heart beats faster during running, exercise is stressful. This is incorrect. During exercise the heart rate increases to send more oxygen to working muscles, but after regular training the resting heart rate becomes lower because the heart has grown stronger and pumps more blood with each beat. The correction is that exercise makes the heart more efficient, not weaker.

Misconception 3: "Repeating the same healthy habit in different words gives more marks." This matches the board examiner observation that students often lose marks by writing the same point again instead of adding a new one. For example, writing "do exercise" and then "play games" is really only one point, because playing games is a kind of exercise. The correction is to give distinct, separate habits such as regular exercise, balanced diet, adequate sleep, avoiding smoking, and drinking water, each with its own explanation.
diagnosticText:
Q1 (recall): List four habits that help keep the heart healthy.
Answer: Four important habits that help keep the heart healthy are regular exercise, a balanced diet, adequate sleep, and avoiding smoking and junk food. Regular exercise, which is also called physical activity, strengthens the heart muscle and improves the flow of blood through the blood vessels. When a child runs, jumps, swims, or plays a sport, the heart pumps faster for a short time and gradually becomes stronger. A balanced diet means eating a variety of fresh fruits and vegetables, whole grains such as wheat, rice, ragi, and jowar, pulses such as moong and rajma, a small amount of healthy fat, and drinking enough water. This gives the body good nutrition and prevents too much fat and cholesterol from collecting inside the blood vessels. Adequate sleep means sleeping about eight to ten hours so that the heart and the whole body can rest and repair themselves. Avoiding smoking, tobacco, and too much junk food protects the lungs and the inner lining of the blood vessels from damage. When these four habits are followed together, the heart stays strong and pumps blood efficiently.

Q2 (reasoning): Explain how regular exercise helps the heart pump blood more efficiently.
Answer: Regular exercise helps the heart pump blood more efficiently because it trains the heart muscle, just as practice trains the muscles of the arms and legs. The heart is made of cardiac muscle, and like any other muscle it becomes stronger when it is used regularly. During exercise, the body needs more oxygen, so the heart beats faster to send more blood to the muscles. With repeated exercise, the heart muscle grows thicker and stronger, and the chambers can hold and pump a larger amount of blood with each beat. Because each beat moves more blood, the heart does not need to beat as many times when a person is resting. This lower resting heart rate is a sign of good cardiovascular fitness. Exercise also helps the blood vessels stay wide and flexible, so blood can flow easily. It helps control body weight and blood pressure, which means the heart does not have to work against extra fat or high pressure. In short, exercise makes the heart a stronger, more efficient pump and keeps the blood vessels healthy.

Q3 (evaluate): A student says, "It is enough to eat only fruits to keep the heart healthy." Evaluate this statement.
Answer: This statement is partially correct but not fully correct, so it should be carefully evaluated. It is true that eating fruits is very good for the heart. Fruits such as oranges, guava, papaya, and banana contain vitamins, minerals, water, and fibre that help the blood vessels stay healthy and prevent cholesterol from building up. Fibre in fruits also helps remove some fat from the digestive system. However, the statement is wrong if it means that only fruits are needed. The heart needs many other nutrients to stay healthy. Vegetables provide different vitamins and minerals. Whole grains such as wheat, rice, oats, and millets give energy. Pulses, milk, eggs, and fish give proteins for building and repairing the heart muscle and blood vessels. A small amount of healthy fat from nuts, seeds, and cooking oils is also needed for the body to work well. Drinking water helps the blood flow easily. If a person ate only fruits, the body would miss proteins, some vitamins, and enough energy for exercise and daily work. Therefore, a balanced diet, not just fruits, is needed for a healthy heart. The best habit is to eat a variety of foods in the right amounts, with plenty of fruits and vegetables as part of that variety.

Q4 (apply): Imagine your friend Priya spends three hours every day watching television and eats chips, fried noodles, and sugary drinks. Suggest a one-day heart-healthy plan for her.
Answer: A one-day heart-healthy plan for Priya should include small changes in eating, activity, sleep, and water. In the morning, she can start with a glass of water and a breakfast of poha or idli with vegetables and a small bowl of fruit such as papaya or banana. Instead of chips while watching television, she can keep a bowl of roasted makhana, peanuts, or sliced cucumber nearby. For lunch, she can have chapati, dal, a bowl of rice, a vegetable curry such as cabbage, carrots, or beans, and a small serving of curd. In the evening, she should replace at least one hour of television with outdoor activity. She can walk in the park, skip rope, cycle, or play badminton with a friend for thirty to forty minutes. This physical activity will help her heart become stronger and will reduce the time she spends sitting. For dinner, she can eat roti, a light vegetable dish, and a small portion of dal. She should drink six to eight glasses of water during the day and avoid sugary colas. Finally, she should sleep by nine-thirty or ten o'clock so that her heart and body get enough rest. This plan is practical because it does not stop all television at once, but it adds healthy food, exercise, water, and sleep step by step.

Q5 (create): Design a poster for your school that tells students three simple ways to keep the heart healthy. What will you draw and write?
Answer: My poster will be titled "Love Your Heart, Live Active!" and it will show three simple ways to keep the heart healthy. At the top I will draw a big, smiling heart with strong arms and legs to show that the heart is a muscle. The first section will show a child cycling to school and children playing kho-kho in a playground. The caption will read, "Move Every Day: Walk, cycle, or play for at least one hour. Your heart gets stronger with every game." The second section will show a colourful plate filled with chapati, dal, green vegetables, sliced fruits, and a glass of water. The caption will be, "Eat a Rainbow: Fill half your plate with fruits and vegetables, eat whole grains, and drink water instead of sugary drinks." The third section will show a child sleeping peacefully in a bed with a moon outside the window, and a "no smoking" sign. The caption will be, "Rest and Refuse: Sleep eight to ten hours, say no to smoking and tobacco, and choose healthy snacks over junk food." At the bottom of the poster I will write the line, "A healthy heart starts with small habits." This poster is attractive, clear, and uses pictures to help all students remember the message even if they only glance at it.
masteryCriteria: Can list three habits for a healthy heart (exercise, low-fat diet, no smoking); can state two causes of heart disease (high cholesterol, lack of exercise); can explain why regular exercise strengthens the heart.

title: Skin and its functions - protection, sensation, temperature regulation
definition:
The skin is the largest organ of the human body and forms the first line of defence between the inside of the body and the outside world. It is not a single sheet but a complex organ made up of two main layers. The outer, thinner layer is the epidermis, built from many rows of tough, flattened, dead and living cells. These cells are packed tightly together so that water, dust, disease-causing microbes, and many harmful chemicals cannot pass through easily. The epidermis therefore acts as a physical barrier that protects the softer tissues underneath from mechanical injury such as cuts, friction, and pressure. Buried in the lower part of the epidermis are cells called melanocytes, which make a dark brown pigment called melanin. Melanin gives the skin its colour and acts like natural sunscreen by absorbing dangerous ultraviolet, or UV, radiation from sunlight. People with darker skin have more melanin, which gives them greater protection against the strong tropical sun in places such as Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu, while lighter skin contains less melanin and burns more quickly.

Beneath the epidermis is the dermis, a thicker layer made of connective tissue and containing blood vessels, nerve endings, sweat glands, and hair roots. The nerve endings in the dermis make the skin a sense organ; they detect touch, pressure, pain, heat, and cold and send messages to the brain so that we can respond. For example, pulling the hand away from a hot tawa on a kitchen stove is possible because these nerve endings send a pain message within a fraction of a second. The dermis also contains coiled sweat glands that open onto the surface through tiny pores. When the body becomes too warm, these glands release sweat, which is mostly water with small amounts of salts and urea. As the sweat evaporates from the skin, it takes heat away and cools the body. At the same time, the blood vessels near the skin surface dilate, or widen, allowing more warm blood to flow near the surface so that heat can escape. When it is cold, the blood vessels constrict, or narrow, keeping warm blood deeper inside the body, and shivering in the muscles generates extra heat. In this way the skin is the body's natural air-conditioner. Because sweat carries away small quantities of urea and salts, the skin also contributes to excretion. Finally, the skin can make vitamin D when sunlight strikes it, especially in the early morning or late afternoon. Vitamin D is needed for the absorption of calcium and for strong bones and teeth, so the skin is also a small chemical factory. In short, the epidermis, dermis, melanin, sweat glands, nerve endings, and blood vessels are all structures that make the skin a multifunctional organ.

Q1 (recall): Name the two main layers of the skin and list the five main functions of the skin. For each function, name one structure in the skin that supports it.
Answer: The skin is made up of the outer epidermis and the inner dermis. Its five main functions are protection, sensation, temperature regulation, excretion, and vitamin D synthesis. Protection is supported by the epidermis, whose tightly packed cells form a barrier against microbes and mechanical injury, and by melanin, which absorbs UV radiation. Sensation is supported by nerve endings in the dermis that detect touch, pressure, pain, heat, and cold. Temperature regulation is supported by sweat glands in the dermis, which release sweat that cools the body by evaporation, and by blood vessels that dilate or constrict to control heat loss. Excretion is supported by sweat glands, which remove small amounts of urea and salts. Vitamin D synthesis is supported by skin cells in the epidermis and dermis that use sunlight to make vitamin D, needed for strong bones and teeth.

Q2 (reasoning): Explain why a person who has just run a race on a hot day in Mumbai starts sweating and the skin looks flushed. What would happen if the body could not sweat?
Answer: When a person runs, the muscles produce a lot of heat, raising body temperature. To stop overheating, the skin's sweat glands in the dermis release sweat onto the skin surface. As the water in sweat evaporates, it takes away heat and cools the body. At the same time, the blood vessels near the skin surface dilate, or widen, so more warm blood flows close to the surface, making the skin look flushed and allowing heat to escape into the air. This is the skin's temperature regulation in action. If the body could not sweat, heat would build up inside. The body temperature could rise to dangerous levels, leading to heat exhaustion or heat stroke. That is why sweating is not just uncomfortable; it is essential for survival in hot climates.

Q3 (evaluate): A classmate says, "The skin is just a wrapper. Its only real job is to make us look good and feel touch. The heart, lungs, and stomach are far more important, so we do not need to learn about sweat glands or melanin." Evaluate this statement, giving a balanced argument.
Answer: This statement is partly true but mostly incorrect. It is true that the skin gives us our appearance and allows us to feel touch, pressure, pain, heat, and cold through nerve endings in the dermis. It is also true that organs like the heart, lungs, and stomach are vital. However, the claim that the skin is "just a wrapper" is wrong because the skin performs many other life-supporting jobs. The skin protects the body from microbes, UV radiation, and mechanical injury through the epidermis and melanin. It regulates temperature through sweating and blood-vessel changes, which is essential for enzymes and cells to work. It helps remove small amounts of waste through sweat, and it makes vitamin D when sunlight falls on it, which is needed for calcium absorption and strong bones. Without the skin, the heart and lungs would also be in danger because infections and injuries could enter the body easily, and body temperature could become uncontrolled. Therefore, the skin is not the only important organ, but it is an important organ that works together with the heart, lungs, and stomach to keep the body alive and healthy. We certainly need to learn about sweat glands and melanin.

Q4 (apply): On a hot afternoon in May, you are playing cricket in the school ground in Delhi. Your coach tells you to drink water, wear a cap, and rest in the shade. Using your knowledge of how the skin cools the body, explain why each of these advice is useful and what could happen if you ignore it.
Answer: In the Delhi summer, the body gains a lot of heat from the sun and from exercise. The skin tries to cool the body by releasing sweat and by dilating blood vessels so that heat can escape. Drinking water is important because sweat is mainly water; if the body loses too much water without replacing it, there will not be enough water left to make sweat, so the skin cannot cool the body effectively. Wearing a cap reduces direct sunlight on the head, which means the skin receives less UV radiation and less heat, so it does not have to work as hard. Resting in the shade lowers the amount of heat the body is taking in, giving the skin time to remove the heat that is already inside. If a student ignores all three, the skin's temperature regulation may fail. The person could become dehydrated, stop sweating, overheat, and suffer heat exhaustion or sunstroke. The skin's sweat glands need support from behaviour to do their job well.

Q5 (create): Design a one-day "Skin Smart Summer" camp plan for Class 6 students in an Indian city. Your plan must include (a) one activity that shows how melanin protects against UV rays, (b) one activity that explains why we sweat, and (c) one message about vitamin D and safe sun exposure.
Answer: The camp could run from 9 a.m. to 12 p.m. in a school garden, avoiding the peak afternoon sun. For the melanin activity, students could use dark and light coloured paper placed under a magnifier in sunlight; the darker paper heats up more, showing that darker surfaces absorb more energy, just as melanin absorbs UV rays. The teacher should explain that melanin is the body's natural sunscreen and that wearing full-sleeved cotton clothes gives extra protection. For the sweating activity, students could measure the temperature of a wet cloth and a dry cloth under a fan; the wet cloth becomes cooler because evaporation removes heat, just as sweat cools the skin. They could also taste a drop of sweat to notice the salty taste, which shows that urea and salts leave the body. The vitamin D message could be: "Spend 15--20 minutes in the morning sun before 10 a.m. to help your skin make vitamin D for strong bones, but avoid the midday sun because too much UV can burn the skin." At the end, students could make a poster with the five skin functions and one summer safety tip.
